AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To describe changes in health-related quality of life (HRQL) over time in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), relative to other outcomes; to identify predictors of unfavourable HRQL trajectories.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Children with JIA in the Research in Arthritis in Canadian Children emphasizing Outcomes (ReACCh-Out) cohort were included. The Juvenile Arthritis Quality of Life Questionnaire (JAQQ, a standardized instrument), health-related Quality of My Life (HRQoML, an instrument based on personal valuations) and JIA core variables were completed serially. Analyses included median values, Kaplan-Meier survival curves, and latent trajectory analysis.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: 1249 patients enrolled at a median of 0.5 months after diagnosis were followed for a median of 34.2 months. The degree of initial HRQL impairment and probabilities of reaching the best possible HRQL scores varied across JIA categories (best for oligoarthritis, worst for RF-positive polyarthritis). Median times to attain best possible HRQL scores (JAQQ 59.3, HRQoML 34.5 months), lagged behind those for disease activity, pain, and disability measures. Most patients followed trajectories with minimal or mild impairment; however, 7.6% and 13.8% of patients, respectively, followed JAQQ and HRQoML trajectories with persistent major impairment in HRQL. JIA category, aboriginal ethnicity, and baseline disease activity measures distinguished between membership in trajectories with major and minimal impairments.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Improvement in HRQL is slower than for disease activity, pain, and disability. Improvement of a measure based on respondents' preferences (HRQoML) is more rapid than that of a standardized measure (JAQQ). Higher disease activity at diagnosis heralds an unfavourable HRQL trajectory. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
